summary: This best current practice says IPv6 support is no longer optional for IP-capable nodes, given the shortage of IPv4 space and the limits of transition technologies. It also warns that older IETF documents using the word IP may be misread as IPv4 only.

eli5.summary: The old internet addresses are running out. This tells builders that every new device must also know the new addresses.

questions: ipv6 required for all ip nodes
is ipv6 support mandatory for new devices
what is dual stack ipv4 and ipv6
subtitle: IPv6 support is no longer optional: new IP implementations must support it and must not require IPv4.

tldr.problem: IPv4 addresses have run out, yet many vendors still sell Internet-capable devices without IPv6, and older IETF documents use the word IP in ways that can mean IPv4 only.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC states best practices: new IP implementations must support IPv6, updates should, and IPv6 must be at least as good as IPv4 and must not depend on IPv4.
tldr.outcome: It warns implementers to check whether a given standard covers IPv6 and to use the IPv6 requirements documents as companions.

today: RFC 6540 is a Best Current Practice published in April 2012. According to the metadata for this page it has not been obsoleted or updated. The current IPv6 requirements it points to are RFC 6434 and RFC 6204.

sections.title: Why IPv6 Can No Longer Be Optional
sections.content:
RFC 6540 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 177). It observes that IPv4 has connected hosts for over 30 years, but billions of hosts now need unique addresses. The IANA global pool of IPv4 addresses has been exhausted, and the free pool of each Regional Internet Registry will follow, starting with APNIC.

Transition technologies that stretch the life of IPv4 exist, but nearly all come with trade-offs that make them worse long-term answers than deploying IPv6. The RFC points to RFC 6269 for discussion of the issues with address sharing.
sections.eli5: The old addresses ran out, and patches to make them last longer all have downsides. The new addresses are the lasting fix.

sections.title: The Deployment Problem
sections.content:
IPv6 was proposed in 1995 in RFC 1883 and has been refined since, for example in RFC 2460. Yet deployment has been held back by uneven hardware and software support. Many vendors, especially in the consumer space, treat IPv6 as optional and still sell "IP-capable" or "Internet-Capable" devices without it. They also choose not to update the software on devices that could be updated.

The RFC argues the hardware refresh cycle alone will not fix this in a reasonable time. Consumers do not buy based on IPv6 support and will not replace working devices just to add it, and the network operator often has no control over what the consumer buys. The lack of support makes the transition harder and drives the need for expensive, complicated technologies to keep IPv4-only devices going and to interwork IPv4-only and IPv6-only hosts. IPv4 is expected to coexist with IPv6 for many years, but the sooner most devices support IPv6, the shorter the transition.
sections.eli5: Shops keep selling gadgets that only know the old addresses, and people keep using them. That makes the switch slower and costlier.

sections.title: When "IP" Means IPv4
sections.content:
The IETF wrote IPv6 as a completely separate set of standalone documents rather than updating the IPv4 specifications. Many early documents use "IP" to mean IPv4, so today "IP" could mean IPv4 plus IPv6, IPv6 only, or IPv4 only.

The RFC gives examples. RFC 1812, an IPv4 router specification, uses generic "IP" in Sections 1, 2 and 4. RFC 1122 is no longer a complete definition of the Internet protocol suite because it omits IPv6: Section 3.2 is an IPv4-only walk-through, and Section 3.2.1.1 explicitly requires discarding an IP datagram whose version number is not 4, which would be harmful to IPv6 forwarding.

Implementers are therefore cautioned to know whether a given standard includes or excludes IPv6, and to use the informative references as companion guidelines when it does not define both. Current IPv6 requirements are in RFC 6204 and RFC 6434.
sections.eli5: Old rulebooks say just "IP" when they only mean the old kind. Builders have to check which kind a rule is really about.

sections.title: The Best Practices
sections.content:
The RFC lists five practices:

  • New IP implementations must support IPv6.
  • Updates to current IP implementations should support IPv6.
  • IPv6 support must be equivalent or better in quality and functionality than IPv4 support in a new or updated implementation.
  • New and updated IP networking implementations should support IPv4 and IPv6 coexistence (dual-stack), but must not require IPv4 for proper and complete function.
  • Implementers are encouraged to update existing hardware and software to enable IPv6 wherever technically feasible.

To ensure interoperability, implementers building IP nodes need to support both IPv4 and IPv6.
sections.eli5: New gadgets must speak the new address language, and it must work as well as the old one. They should not need the old one to work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document generates no direct security considerations. The existing, documented security considerations for implementing IPv6 apply.

The RFC is advisory guidance and defines no protocol messages, formats or registries.
sections.eli5: This note adds no new safety rules. The usual safety advice for the new addresses still applies.

viz.caption: THE FIVE BEST PRACTICES IN SHORT

items.title: Quality
items.text: IPv6 must be equivalent or better than IPv4.

items.title: Dual-stack
items.text: Should coexist with IPv4, but must not require IPv4.

items.title: Existing gear
items.text: Update to enable IPv6 where technically feasible.
